subject.title: Valéry as Dictator
subject.author: Amiri Baraka
subject.text:
Sad. And it comes tomorrow. Again, gray, the streaks of work shredding the stone of the pavement, dissolving  with the idea of singular endeavor.  Herds, the herds of suffering intelligences bunched, and out of  hearing. Though the day come to us                     in waves,                                        sun, air, the beat
of the clock.                        Though I stare at the radical  world,               wishing it would stand still.                                                                  Tell me, and I gain at the telling. Of the lie, and the waking
against the heavy breathing
of new light, dawn, shattering
the naive cluck
of feeling.                    What is tomorrow   that it cannot come                                      today?

title: The Dictator This Poem Was Built to Disobey
standfirst: LeRoi Jones named this poem after Paul Valéry, the most rigorously self-controlled poet in modern French letters, then wrote it in the loose, breath-spaced style of the Black Mountain poets who stood for everything Valéry rejected. He collected it in The Dead Lecturer in 1964, a year before the assassination of Malcolm X ended this version of his career outright.

sections.heading: A Dictator Who Leaves No Mark
sections.body:
Read the poem before reading anything written about it, and the title starts to look like a joke nobody has explained. "Valéry as Dictator" promises rule, a single hand pressing down on the material. What is actually on the page is the opposite: sentences that drift out of grammar and back in, no rhyme, no stanza, no metre holding one line to the next, and gaps between words wide enough to read as silence rather than spacing.

> Though the day come to us                     in waves,                                        sun, air, the beat
> of the clock.

Those gaps are not typographical accidents. They are the entire method of the poem. Something written under an actual dictator's rule would look like a straight line, obedient margin to obedient margin. This one keeps stopping to breathe instead. Whoever is being named dictator in the title, it plainly is not in charge of how this poem moves.

sections.heading: The Machine Olson Handed Him
sections.body:
The gaps have an author, and it isn't Valéry. In 1950 Charles Olson published "Projective Verse," the essay that became close to a founding manifesto for the loose alliance of writers known as the Black Mountain poets. Olson's argument was that a poem should be scored for the voice the way music is scored for an instrument, with the typed page standing in for the score: he wrote that the typewriter had "ready to hand" a way to fix on paper "the breath, the pauses, the suspensions" a poet actually intended, because its rigid grid of character-widths let a writer mark exactly how long a silence should run.

Jones knew this doctrine from the inside, not as a fan reading it secondhand. His own magazine, Yugen, and its mimeographed successor, The Floating Bear, had been publishing Olson himself for years, alongside Diane di Prima, Allen Ginsberg and Gary Snyder. Critics have since read The Dead Lecturer as a book that turns the avant-garde's own tools against the avant-garde — indicting the tradition it is written entirely inside. A poem that borrows Olson's spacing to argue with Valéry's name is that fight in miniature.

sections.heading: The Man Whose Name Meant Control
sections.body:
Valéry earned the association with control long before Jones wrote a line about him. After an early burst of poems in his twenties, Valéry stopped publishing for two decades and spent the time on something closer to research than writing: from 1894 until his death he rose at dawn most days to work through pages of notebooks, later collected as the Cahiers, on method, consciousness and the mechanics of language — treating a poem as a problem for a fully awake, watchful mind to solve, not something delivered to it. He was openly hostile to the idea of inspiration, and the Surrealists, who had built an entire practice on trusting exactly that, returned the hostility without much subtlety of their own.

By the time Jones was a teenager, France had made that discipline close to official. The Académie française elected Valéry in 1925; the Collège de France created a chair in poetry in 1937 with no candidate but him in mind. A poet who worked from suspicion of spontaneity, and ended up crowned by the state for it, is a reasonable person to call, half-admiringly, a dictator.

sections.heading: The Only Black Poet in the Room
sections.body:
When Jones wrote this, he was not visiting the avant-garde Olson represented — he was one of its editors. Donald Allen's 1960 anthology The New American Poetry, the book that first drew a public map of the Beats, the New York School and the Black Mountain poets as a single movement, included exactly one Black contributor: Jones. He had married Hettie Cohen in 1958; together they ran Yugen and Totem Press out of their own apartment, and he co-edited The Floating Bear with di Prima. By his own account he was, in these years, "smack in the center" of the Lower East Side scene, at the same late-night parties as the white poets he was publishing.

His own working idea of what a poem should do sat closer to Olson's camp than to Valéry's. "Let my poems be a graph / of me," he wrote in another poem from the same book, "Balboa, the Entertainer" — poetry as a direct trace of a particular, specific nervous system, not, as Valéry wanted, evidence of a mind that had learned to master its own noise.

sections.heading: What Tomorrow Can't Wait For
sections.body:
The poem's own argument arrives only at the very end, after four sentences that go nowhere in particular: "What is tomorrow   that it cannot come                                      today?" It is a strange question to hang a title about dictatorship on — no ruler, no decree, just an impatience with delay stated as a flat demand. In 2013, a year after Baraka's death, the poet Thomas Sayers Ellis chose this poem over better-known ones to set to music with the saxophonist James Brandon Lewis, because that closing line held, in his words, "the re-starting protest point of the tradition and the unconditioned condition of a pure philosophy of all breathing Blackness."

The wait the poem complains about turned out to be short. The Dead Lecturer appeared in 1964, the same year Jones's play Dutchman won an Obie for Best American Play. A year later, Malcolm X was assassinated; Jones changed his name to Amiri Baraka, left the Lower East Side, and founded the Black Arts Repertory Theater in Harlem. The avant-garde he had helped build, and the dictator's name he had borrowed to argue with it, both went the same way afterward: dropped, on a schedule the poem itself had already run out of patience with.
